sections.bodyAdd: The chapter as a whole has two jobs, and this module covers the first half of both. One job is to say more about **God’s nature** — what the cause reached by the proofs must be like. The other is to say more about **God’s causal relationship to the world** — how such a cause acts on and sustains things (taken up mostly in Part B). Feser stresses that the earlier chapters already said something about both; the aim now is to be systematic. His method is to reason from the world *considered as an effect* to the nature of its *cause*, and since that kind of reasoning depends on general principles about causes and about language, he states and defends those principles before deriving a single attribute.
sections.takeaway: Each proof already reached a cause with a specific nature; this chapter systematically unpacks that nature and shows it is one and the same God, reasoning from the world as effect to God as cause.
sections.deepDive:
The hardest idea in this opening is easy to miss: **how can we know anything about the nature of a cause we never observe?** Many people assume that cosmological arguments, at best, get you “some first cause or other,” and that a separate, shakier leap is needed to get from there to God. Philosophers sometimes call this the “gap problem.” Feser’s recap is quietly setting up his answer.

Notice what each proof actually concluded. The Aristotelian proof didn’t end with “something started things off” but with a *purely actual* actualizer — something with no unrealized potential. The Neo-Platonic proof ended with something *absolutely simple*. The Augustinian proof ended with an *intellect* in which necessary truths exist. The Thomistic proof ended with *subsistent existence itself*. The rationalist proof ended with an *absolutely necessary* being. These are not bare placeholders; they are descriptions with content. The work of this chapter is to draw out what that content implies, not to bolt new features onto an empty “first cause.”

A thought experiment helps. Suppose a detective finds that a safe was opened without force, by someone who knew the combination, left no fingerprints, and was inside a locked building overnight. She hasn’t seen the culprit, but the *features of the effect* sharply constrain what the cause could be. Feser’s approach is similar, only more rigorous: the relevant features are metaphysical (potency being actualized, composition, dependence of existence), and the constraints follow by strict reasoning.

Two nuances. First, Feser admits he has already said things about God’s nature in earlier chapters; this chapter is a systematic treatment, not a first attempt. Second, he announces that general principles must come first — proportionate causality, “action follows being,” and the analogy of being — because inferring from effect to cause and describing a cause radically unlike its effects both require them.

In the formal reasoning, this section supplies **step 1**: the five conclusions taken as data. Everything later — unity (step 21), convergence (step 26), simplicity (step 30), and the rest — is an unpacking of step 1 with the help of steps 2–13.

The usual confusion: people think that because the proofs are *about existence*, they say nothing about *character*. But “purely actual,” “simple,” and “necessary” are already characterizations. The question is only how far they reach — and the answer, this chapter argues, is: very far.

checks.q: Which of the five proofs, as Feser recaps them, begins from abstract objects such as numbers and propositions?
options: The Aristotelian proof
The Neo-Platonic proof
The Augustinian proof
The rationalist proof
checks.explanation: The Augustinian proof argues from abstract objects to a divine intellect in which they exist as ideas. The Aristotelian starts from change; the Neo-Platonic from composition; the rationalist from PSR.

checks.q: Why does Feser lay out general principles before deriving any divine attribute?
options: Because inferring the nature of a cause from the world as its effect depends on general principles about causes and language
Because the attributes follow from Scripture, which the principles interpret
Because the principles are needed to prove God exists in the first place
Because the attributes are arbitrary unless defined by convention
checks.explanation: The chapter reasons from the world, considered as an effect, to its cause; that requires principles like PPC and the analogy of being. God’s existence was already argued for in chapters 1–5.

sections.bodyAdd: Two features of the principle deserve emphasis. First, it concerns the **total** cause — all the factors that together produce the effect — not any single ingredient. Second, the three modes show that PPC is not a demand that causes *resemble* their effects. What is ruled out is only that the effect should contain something for which nothing in the total cause accounts. Applied to God, this will mean that the perfections found in creatures must be present in their First Cause — but eminently, in a higher way, not as the limited, material features we meet in things.
sections.takeaway: PPC says an effect’s features must be in its total cause formally, virtually, or eminently — not that the cause must resemble the effect — and it follows from PC and PSR.
sections.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the difference between **virtual** and **eminent** presence, and why neither is a cheat.

Start with the $20 example and ask, in each case, *what exactly does the cause have?* In the formal case, I have the very thing you get: a bill. In the virtual case, I have no bill but I have a *power or resource* — funds and a bank that will convert them into a bill in your hands. What is in the effect is in the total cause, but in the mode of a capacity rather than a finished feature. In the eminent case, I have something more fundamental still: control over the process by which bills are made at all. The eminent cause does not merely have *a* $20 potential; it has the source of all such bills.

A second worked example: a sculptor produces a statue with a certain shape. The sculptor doesn’t *have* that shape (formal presence fails — he isn’t shaped like a horse). But the shape is in the total cause — his idea and skill, the chisel, the marble’s capacity to be cut — virtually. And a being who could produce not just this statue but marble, sculptors, and shape itself would contain the statue’s perfection eminently.

Why isn’t this a trick to make PPC unfalsifiable? Because each mode still requires *something real* in the cause that accounts for the effect. A person with no bill, no funds, and no press cannot give you $20. That is exactly what PPC predicts. The principle rules out effects exceeding the resources of their total causes; it does not rule out causes that are richer than, or different in kind from, their effects.

The grounding is simple. If some feature of an effect had no source in its total cause, then a potential would have been actualized by nothing (against the principle of causality, from chapter 1), and that feature would have no explanation (against PSR, from chapter 5). That is the reasoning behind **step 3**; the three modes are the content of **step 2**.

The usual confusion: people hear “a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have” and conclude that a creator of material, changing things must itself be material and changing. But material and changeable features can be in God *eminently* — as the power to produce and sustain such things — without God being material. Later, PPC also helps explain why the First Cause must contain, in a higher way, perfections like intellect (a theme of Part B).

checks.q: A city council has no parks but has the legal authority and budget to create them. The parks it later creates were in the council:
options: Formally
Not at all, so PPC is violated
Only metaphorically
Virtually (as power and resources), not formally
checks.explanation: The council doesn’t have parks, but its budget and authority are a real capacity that accounts for them — the virtual mode, like my bank account in Feser’s example.

checks.q: Why does Feser think PPC follows from the principle of causality and PSR?
options: Because both principles say effects must resemble causes
Because an effect-feature with no source in its total cause would be an actualization with no actualizer and a fact with no explanation
Because PSR is defined as PPC applied to material things
Because PC applies only to God and PSR only to creatures
checks.explanation: That is the core of step 3. Neither PC nor PSR says effects resemble causes.

checks.q: What does the eminent case in the $20 example add beyond the virtual case?
options: The cause has something more fundamental than the effect’s feature: the power to make things of that kind
The cause has more $20 bills than in the formal case
The effect is only imaginary
The cause is identical to the effect
checks.explanation: Access to the press is not having money but having the power to make money — the mark of eminent presence.

sections.bodyAdd: The shape of Feser’s reply is worth noticing. He does not deny that the cake’s sponginess is genuinely new, or that helium’s properties differ from hydrogen’s. He denies only that such novelty arises from nothing in the total cause. The objection works only by quietly replacing the principle defenders actually hold with a cruder one.
sections.takeaway: Cottingham refutes a straw man: PPC concerns the total cause and allows virtual and eminent presence, and explaining by potentialities is minimally informative, not trivial.
sections.deepDive:
The subtle part of this section is the **triviality charge**, because Feser partly agrees with it. Cottingham’s worry is a classic one: if every surprising effect can be “explained” by saying its features were potentially in the cause, hasn’t PPC become empty — true no matter what happens?

Feser’s answer has two layers. First, he openly accepts the language of potentiality. Aquinas himself said that the heat produced in a warmed body was previously in it potentially, and that the agent actualizes it. In the $20 cases, the virtual and eminent explanations *are* explanations in terms of potentialities — the account’s potential to be drawn on, the press’s potential to print. So the defender isn’t sneaking potentiality in to save the principle; it was always part of it.

Second, he distinguishes **minimally informative** from **noninformative**. A course illustration: Molière famously mocked doctors who said opium puts people to sleep because it has a “dormitive power.” The joke lands because the explanation is thin. But it is not empty: it tells you the sleepiness comes from something in the opium rather than from the patient’s mood or the weather, and it directs inquiry toward what in opium has that power. Likewise, saying the sponginess was potentially in the ingredients-plus-baking tells you where to look (the chemistry of eggs, flour, heat) and rules out that it came from nothing.

The most convincing evidence of non-triviality comes in the next section: philosophers on opposite sides (Churchland, dualists) draw substantive, disputed conclusions from PPC. A trivial principle can’t settle anything.

Notice also the **straw man** diagnosis. Cottingham’s examples consider only material ingredients. But PPC speaks of the *total* cause. Restricting the principle to ingredients, then refuting the restricted version, attacks something no defender holds. The heirloom reading makes the parallel mistake of assuming formal presence — as if the cook must be spongy. A Thomist writer’s quip about the black eye makes the point memorably.

This section protects **step 2** of the argument (the formulation of PPC) and **step 3** (its grounding).

The usual confusion: people think that because a new feature is *novel*, it must violate PPC. But novelty of instance — a new heat, a new sponginess — is exactly what PPC expects: the total cause actualizes something that was potential. What PPC forbids is only an effect-feature that nothing in the total cause accounts for.

checks.q: Which of Feser’s replies targets the fact that Cottingham’s examples mention only eggs, flour, butter, and hydrogen?
options: The reply that PPC concerns the total cause, not merely the material factors
The reply from the second law of thermodynamics
The reply that sponginess is an illusion
The reply that analogy is literal
checks.explanation: Restricting PPC to material ingredients and refuting that is a straw man; the total cause includes baker, mixing, and heat.

checks.q: What does Aquinas’ example of the hot body show?
options: That heat is literally transferred from one body to another
That a cause produces a numerically new feature by actualizing a potential in the recipient
That PPC applies only to heat
That causes never resemble their effects
checks.explanation: The heating body doesn’t hand over its own heat; it actualizes a new heat that was potential in the heated body.

checks.q: How does Feser respond to the claim that explaining sponginess as “potentially present” makes PPC trivial?
options: He denies that potentiality is involved at all
He concedes PPC is trivial but says trivial truths are useful
He says explanations by potentialities may be minimally informative but are not noninformative
He replaces PPC with the principle of causality
checks.explanation: Feser embraces the language of potentiality but rejects the slide from “minimally informative” to “trivial.”

sections.bodyAdd: Notice what Feser is and is not claiming. He is not using thermodynamics or biology to prove God’s existence. He is showing that PPC is a principle that scientific accounts themselves respect, and that naturalists employ when it suits them — so it can’t be dismissed as a theological invention or a triviality.
sections.takeaway: PPC is substantive and independent of theology: materialists and dualists both argue from it, and even the naturalistic account of evolution respects it.
sections.deepDive:
The key move in this section is **dialectical**: Feser shows that a principle critics call medieval or trivial is actually shared ground.

Consider Churchland’s argument slowly. Premise: human beings, individually and as a species, arise from purely material beginnings (a fertilized egg; early organisms) through purely material processes (cell division; natural selection). Conclusion: human beings are purely material. What licenses that inference? Only the principle that if the *total* cause is wholly material, the effect must be too — a total cause can’t yield what isn’t in it in some way. Without PPC, Churchland’s argument would have no force: the effect might contain something non-material that simply appeared.

Now the dualist. She accepts the same principle but has a different premise: part of the effect (the intellect) is not material. By PPC, then, the total cause of a human being can’t have been purely material. The two sides disagree about the facts, not about the principle. That is Feser’s point: PPC is so far from trivial that it drives a central debate in philosophy of mind.

Next, evolution. The objection says complex organisms come from simpler ones, so the effect exceeds the cause. Feser patiently reconstructs the standard naturalistic account: every species is a variation on genetic material that has existed since life began; a mutation (from a replication copying error, or radiation, or chemical damage) produces a new trait; environmental conditions make it advantageous. The **total cause** of the new variation is the combination of all three. None alone would suffice — and so the new form is not something from nothing.

Feser then adds a supporting point from physicist Paul Davies: denying that a new life form’s information derives from some combination of prior factors, including the environment, would conflict with the second law of thermodynamics, according to which order and information tend to decline in a closed system. The point is about information bookkeeping, not about God.

Two nuances. Feser explicitly speaks of the *standard naturalistic* account, contrasting it with theistic evolutionary theories; he is showing that even the naturalist’s own story honors PPC. And he concludes that PPC is well founded *independently of natural theology*, while noting it will be very useful in reasoning from the world to its cause.

This secures confidence in **steps 2–3**. The usual confusion is to hear Feser as arguing that evolution needs God here. He isn’t; he is arguing that evolution is no counterexample to PPC.

checks.q: What does Feser think Churchland’s argument for materialism shows about PPC?
options: That PPC is false
That PPC is implicitly assumed by naturalists as well as dualists
That PPC applies only to evolution
That PPC entails materialism
checks.explanation: Churchland infers a material effect from a material total cause — PPC. The dualist runs the same principle the other way.

checks.q: On the naturalistic account Feser describes, which factors together form the total cause of a new biological variation?
options: Genetic material alone
Divine intervention and genetic material
Existing genetic material, a mutation, and environmental circumstances
The organism’s desire to adapt
checks.explanation: No one factor suffices; together they account for the variation, so PPC is respected.

checks.q: Why does Feser mention Paul Davies and the second law of thermodynamics?
options: To support the claim that new biological information must derive from some combination of prior factors
To prove that God must have designed life
To show that evolution is false
To argue that the universe had a beginning
checks.explanation: Davies’ point supports PPC’s application to evolution; it isn’t offered as an argument for God.

sections.bodyAdd: The principle will matter a great deal later. It is what blocks the suggestion that a purely actual First Cause could nonetheless *act* in a way that involves unrealized potential (step 15), and it will return in Part B, where Feser argues that since creatures cannot even exist apart from God, they cannot act apart from him either.
sections.takeaway: What a thing does cannot outrun what it is (unless something else makes it); this is PPC’s counterpart for natures and follows from PSR.
sections.deepDive:
The key idea is that *agere sequitur esse* extends the logic of PPC from **efficient causes** to **formal causes**.

Recall the difference. An efficient cause is what produces a thing or a change in it: the baker, the heat, the sculptor. A formal cause is a thing’s nature — what makes it the kind of thing it is. For a human, that is rational animality; for water, whatever makes water water. PPC says an effect can’t exceed its total efficient cause. *Agere sequitur esse* says a thing’s characteristic activities can’t exceed its nature. Just as the effect is “contained” in the cause, a thing’s operations are “contained” in its nature — they flow from it.

Worked example: salt dissolves in water and a stone doesn’t, because of what salt and stone are. Language flows from rationality; you won’t find a dog composing sonnets. If a stone started, all by itself, to take in nutrients and grow, one of two things would be true: either it isn’t really a stone (it was a strange organism all along), or something is happening that nothing about it explains. The first option shows the principle at work (we revise our view of what the thing is); the second would violate PSR. That is exactly the reasoning Feser gives: an activity outrunning its nature would be unintelligible.

The qualification in Feser’s footnote is important. Things can do what exceeds their nature when *another* agent makes them. The puppet’s wooden limbs dance because the puppeteer moves them; a thrown stone flies because it was thrown. The principle is about what a thing can do *on its own*. So apparent exceptions always point to an outside cause — which confirms rather than refutes the principle.

In the formal argument this is **step 4**, and its big payoff is **step 15**: the First Cause’s being is purely actual, so its acting cannot involve potentiality either. There is nothing in a purely actual nature for merely potential activity to “follow” from.

The usual confusion: people read “action follows being” as determinism, as if everything a thing does is fixed by its nature. That’s not the claim. A free rational agent’s choices flow from its rational nature too, and the principle says only that its activities can’t exceed that nature. Another confusion is to think the principle is a mere definition. It isn’t: it is a substantive thesis, grounded in PSR, which even naturalists use (as the next section shows).

checks.q: How does Feser relate agere sequitur esse to PPC?
options: It is PPC applied to final causes
It applies to formal causes (natures) what PPC says about efficient causes
It is the converse of PPC
It replaces PPC for immaterial things
checks.explanation: PPC: effects can’t exceed their efficient causes. Agere sequitur esse: activities can’t exceed their agent’s nature.

checks.q: A thrown stone breaks a window, though breaking windows is not something stones do on their own. Does this violate agere sequitur esse?
options: Yes, so the principle is only approximate
Yes, unless the stone is alive
No, because the principle concerns what a thing does on its own, and the thrower is acting on the stone
No, because breaking windows is part of a stone’s nature
checks.explanation: Like the puppet, the stone exceeds its own powers only because another agent acts on it.

sections.bodyAdd: The logic of Searle’s complaint is worth spelling out: a property is a way a thing is, so a genuinely immaterial property would require its bearer to be, in that respect, immaterial. That is agere sequitur esse (and PPC) applied to the mind. Whatever one concludes about the mind, the example shows that the principle is part of live contemporary debate rather than a museum piece.
sections.takeaway: Aquinas’ argument for the soul and Searle’s critique of property dualism both rely on agere sequitur esse, showing the principle is shared ground rather than a Scholastic relic.
sections.deepDive:
This section’s hardest move is recognizing that Feser is interested in the **conditional**, not the conclusion. He does not use the immortality of the soul as a premise for anything in natural theology. He uses Aquinas and Searle to show that “action follows being” is a principle people actually reason with.

Lay out Aquinas’ argument as a chain. (1) Intellectual activity is essentially immaterial — Aquinas has independent arguments for this, which Feser defends elsewhere. (2) A material thing cannot carry out an immaterial activity (agere sequitur esse). (3) So the human soul, which carries out intellectual activity, is immaterial. (4) Material things tend to decay by coming apart; immaterial things have no such natural tendency. (5) So the soul does not perish when the body does.

A materialist rejects premise 1. But — Feser’s point — she can accept premise 2, and so the conditional: *if* thinking were immaterial, the thinker would be too. The disagreement is over premise 1, not the principle.

Now Searle. Property dualism tries a middle way: no immaterial substance, but some immaterial properties of the brain. Searle presents a dilemma. Take “over and above.” If a mental property really is over and above the brain, it isn’t a property *of* the brain; it’s a separate thing or entity. If it really is a property of the brain, it isn’t over and above it. Other critics add that it’s mysterious how something wholly material could produce immaterial features. Both complaints rest on the idea that what belongs to a thing can’t exceed what that thing is — agere sequitur esse again (and PPC, for the “produce” version).

A worked comparison: imagine claiming that a stone has the property of understanding calculus but is in every respect just a stone. Everyone senses the incoherence — a property of that kind can’t belong to a bearer of that kind. Property dualism, according to its critics, makes the same kind of claim in a subtler way.

Feser explicitly says he isn’t settling the property-dualism dispute. The section supports **step 4** by showing that its principle is widely presupposed, making it unfair to dismiss it as Scholastic dogma.

The usual confusion: people think that invoking Aquinas’ soul argument commits Feser’s proofs to dualism. It doesn’t. The proofs of God don’t depend on the soul’s immateriality; the example is only an illustration of a principle.

checks.q: What does Feser say a materialist can accept about Aquinas’ argument for the soul?
options: The conclusion that the soul survives death
The conditional that if intellectual activity were immaterial, its subject would have to be immaterial
The premise that intellectual activity is immaterial
Nothing, since materialists reject agere sequitur esse
checks.explanation: The materialist denies that thought is immaterial but can grant the conditional, which is the principle at work.

checks.q: What is Searle’s dilemma against property dualism?
options: Either mental properties are physical or God exists
If a mental property is over and above the brain it is a separate entity, and if it is a property of the brain it is not over and above it
Either the mind is a computer or it is a soul
If the brain is material, thought is impossible
checks.explanation: Searle argues the view is unstable; Feser cites this as an implicit use of agere sequitur esse.

checks.q: Why does Feser discuss Aquinas and Searle in a chapter about God’s nature?
options: To prove the soul’s immortality as a premise for God’s existence
To show that agere sequitur esse is a principle many contemporary philosophers implicitly accept
To argue that property dualism is true
To show that materialism is incompatible with evolution
checks.explanation: The examples show the principle is live and shared, not a relic; Feser explicitly declines to settle the mind-body dispute.

sections.bodyAdd:
It helps to have a quick test for each use. If the two uses could be swapped in any sentence without changing what is claimed, they are **univocal**. If knowing one sense gives you no clue to the other, they are **equivocal** — the connection is an accident of the word. If understanding one sense helps you understand the other, because the things are really related, the use is **analogical**. Wine is good in being what wine should be; a man is good in being what a man should be. The same kind of relation holds, realized very differently.

Feser first introduced analogy in chapter 2. What is new here is his claim that the most basic concept of all — **being** — is analogical. That is illustrated by substances and their attributes. Attributes such as color and shape *modify* a substance and *depend* on it, while the substance does not modify anything else in that way. Both are real, but neither in the same way nor in unrelated ways.
sections.takeaway: Besides univocal (same sense) and equivocal (unrelated senses) uses of words, there is a literal analogical use — and “being” itself is used that way.
sections.deepDive:
The difficult idea here is that **analogy is a third kind of literal meaning**, not a fuzzy halfway house or a polite name for metaphor.

Begin with how we actually talk. “Good” applies to wine, knives, arguments, people, and weather. Nobody thinks a good knife and a good man are good in *exactly* the same sense — a knife isn’t honest. But nobody thinks the word is a pun either, like “bat.” There is a common thread: in each case, the thing measures up to what that kind of thing should be. The thread is real, but it is realized differently in each case. That is analogy.

Now apply this to **being**, the most basic concept there is. Take a stone and its gray color. Both are real — the color isn’t an illusion. But the color exists *in* the stone: it modifies the stone and depends on it. The stone doesn’t exist in something else in that way. So “the stone is real” and “its color is real” don’t use “real” univocally. Yet it would be absurd to say the color is real only in the way a baseball bat is a “bat” in the mammal sense — i.e., not really at all. So “being” is said of substance and attribute analogically.

A thought experiment: imagine trying to make “being” univocal by insisting that to be real is to be a self-standing thing. Then colors, shapes, relations, and potentials would all be unreal. Imagine instead making it equivocal. Then saying a color “exists” would tell you nothing about what it is for a stone to exist. Neither fits how reality is structured.

This section supplies part of **step 5** (the three uses of terms) and prepares **steps 6–12**, which argue that “being” must be analogical. It also sets up **step 13** — that talk about God must be analogical — since if even substance and attribute have being analogically, we should hardly expect God and creatures to have it univocally.

The usual confusion: people hear “analogical” and think “not literally true” or “merely an analogy.” But when you say you “see” the solution to a problem, you are not speaking falsely or poetically — you really grasp it — even though your eyes aren’t involved. Analogical language says something true, in a way fitted to the reality described.

checks.q: “There was a bat in the attic” and “He swung the bat” use “bat”:
options: Univocally
Analogically
Equivocally
By analogy of attribution
checks.explanation: The meanings are completely unrelated; knowing one gives no clue to the other.

checks.q: Why does Feser say a stone and its color have being analogically?
options: Because the color is unreal
Because both are real, but the color exists only in and dependent on the stone, while the stone does not exist in another thing that way
Because color and stone belong to the same genus
Because the word “being” is ambiguous like “bat”
checks.explanation: Attributes modify and depend on substances; both are real, neither univocally nor equivocally.

sections.bodyAdd: Two questions sort the cases. **Is the perfection intrinsically in each thing it is said of?** In attribution, no — the food isn’t itself healthy the way George is. **Is the form or nature literally present in each?** In proper proportionality, yes; in metaphorical proportionality, only in one of them. Theology needs both of the literal kinds: proper proportionality lets us say being, goodness, and life are really in God as well as in creatures, each in its own way; attribution lets us see God as the primary analogate of being, with creatures called beings because of their relation to him as cause (Feser’s footnote).
sections.takeaway: Attribution names things by relation to one primary bearer; proper proportionality finds the perfection really in each; metaphorical proportionality finds it literally in only one — and only the first two are literal.
sections.deepDive:
The difficulty in this section is keeping three kinds of analogy distinct, since the examples can blur. A patient way is to use two tests.

**Test 1: Is the perfection intrinsically in each analogate?** With “healthy,” it’s only in George. The food is called healthy because it *causes* health in things like George; the complexion because it is *caused by and a sign of* his health. Take George away and the food isn’t healthy in itself — it has nutrients, but health is a feature of living bodies. So “healthy” works by **attribution**: one **primary analogate**, several **secondary analogates** named by relation to it.

**Test 2: Is the form or nature literally present in each?** With “alive,” said of a plant, a dog, a human, and an angel — yes. Each really has the nature of a living thing, though plant life (nutrition, growth), animal life (plus sensation), human life (plus reason), and angelic life (pure intellect) are very different. This is **proper proportionality**: intrinsic *and* formal in each. With “lion,” said of the zoo animal and brave George — the courage that grounds the usage is intrinsically in George, but the *form* of lionhood is literally in the animal only. That is **improper or metaphorical proportionality**.

So: attribution fails test 1; metaphorical proportionality passes test 1 but fails test 2; proper proportionality passes both.

Why does this matter for God? Suppose we used attribution alone and said “God is good” means only “God causes goodness in creatures.” Then God wouldn’t intrinsically be good, any more than food is intrinsically healthy. Classical theists want more: goodness, being, and life are *really in* God, in the highest way. That is proper proportionality. Yet attribution also applies, because God is the source on which all creaturely being depends, so he is the primary analogate of being (Feser’s footnote 14).

This section completes **step 5** and is what makes **step 13** possible: literal, positive statements about God.

The usual confusion: “All analogy is metaphor.” Feser insists the reverse is the truth: metaphor is one kind of analogy, but the kinds that matter for metaphysics are nonmetaphorical. When Plantinga later describes Aquinas as treating language about God as nonliteral, this is the distinction he misses.

checks.q: “This food is healthy” is an example of which kind of analogy?
options: Proper proportionality
Attribution, with the food as a secondary analogate
Metaphorical proportionality
Univocal predication
checks.explanation: Health is intrinsically only in the living body (George); food is called healthy as a cause of it.

checks.q: What makes “life” said of plants and angels an analogy of proper proportionality rather than metaphor?
options: Life exists only in angels
The form of being alive is literally present in each, though realized differently
Plants are called alive only because they cause life
The word “life” is ambiguous
checks.explanation: Proper proportionality: the perfection is intrinsic and formal in each analogate.

checks.q: Why would the analogy of attribution alone be inadequate for saying “God is good”?
options: Because it would make “good” univocal
Because it would only mean God causes goodness, not that goodness is intrinsically in God
Because God is a secondary analogate
Because attribution is always metaphorical
checks.explanation: Attribution names secondary analogates by relation without intrinsic possession; classical theists hold that perfections are really in God (proper proportionality), with attribution also applying.
